SysNDD: A Systematic Database for
Neurodevelopmental Disorders
Bernt Popp ,1,2,3,4,* Simon Früh,5,6 Melek Firat Altay ,5,6,7 Hilde Van Esch ,8 Almuth Caliebe ,9 Nuria C. Bramswig ,10 Fabian Hummel ,11 Sopio Gverdtsiteli ,12,13 Tjitske Kleefstra ,14 Annette Schenck ,15,16 Zeynep Tümer ,12,17 Alain Verloes ,18 Christiane Zweier ,5,6

*Correspondence: bernt.popp@charite.de
Abstract
Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous,
and evidence linking additional genes to disease evolves rapidly. We developed
SysNDD, an open-access, expert-curated resource that represents distinct


gene-inheritance-disease associations as entities with standardized confidence,
phenotype, and variant annotations. Each entity retains its curation history, so its
evidence category can change as evidence accumulates. Currently, SysNDD contains
4,275 entities curated from 4,932 publications. Of these, 3,758 entities involving 3,271
genes describe NDDs; the remainder record non-NDD disorders, nearly all linked to
NDD-associated genes, included for completeness. Regarding NDD evidence
categories, 1,838 genes are Definitive, 179 Moderate, 1,248 Limited, and 6 Refuted.
The entity model captures inheritance-specific disorders, including 220 genes with both
autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive NDD associations. Comparison with
seven other NDD gene resources showed complementary coverage, and evidence
categories largely agreed with those of ClinGen, Gene2Phenotype, and PanelApp for
shared gene-disease pairs. NDD genes formed distinct molecular modules, whereas
associated disorders formed broad, overlapping phenotype groups that corresponded
to those modules only selectively. SysNDD provides a continuously maintained,
programmatically accessible framework for gene-disease evidence assessment,
inheritance-aware interpretation, and systematic NDD research.
Introduction
High-throughput sequencing is now considered standard for diagnosing rare genetic
diseases. It has been particularly successful in neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs),
where trio-based exome or genome sequencing identifies a causative variant in more
than 40% of cases1. Large-scale de novo and rare-variant studies continue to expand
the candidate-gene landscape for neurodevelopmental delay and autism2,3. Through
large consortia and matchmaking platforms, international collaborations have identified
many new NDD-associated genes and raised the diagnostic yield4. New classes of
disease genes also continue to emerge, including non-coding genes such as RNU4-2,
which encodes the spliceosomal U4 snRNA5. As a result, NDDs are among the most
clinically and molecularly heterogeneous groups of monogenic disease, with one of the
most rapidly evolving genetic landscapes.
This heterogeneity is evident when comparing published numbers of NDD genes
before and after the advent of large-scale exome sequencing studies such as the


Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) study1. Before large-scale sequencing,
approximately 300 genes had been reported for NDDs6,7. As of September 21, 2026,
SysNDD, the resource presented here, records more than 1,800 genes with a Definitive
NDD association, a number that continues to grow. SysNDD contains more than 1,200
further genes whose strongest NDD association is so far Limited. Gene-disease
associations outnumber genes, because a gene can be linked to multiple diseases, not
all of which include developmental delay/intellectual disability (ID). Maintaining current,
expert-curated, and complementary resources is therefore essential to inform accurate
diagnostics and clinical research8.
Existing gene knowledge databases include generalized catalogs of rare disease
associations such as Orphanet9 and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM)10,
diagnostic gene panels (e.g., PanelApp11), and specialized NDD-focused gene-validity
resources such as Gene2Phenotype12 and SFARI13. However, these curation efforts
differ in scope, evidence standards, and interoperability. Standardization initiatives
such as the ClinGen framework14,15 and the Gene Curation Coalition (GenCC)16,17
have helped harmonize gene-disease validity assessment across resources. Against
this background, SysNDD provides a disease-centered NDD resource with
standardized phenotype and variant annotations, evidence categories broadly
comparable to ClinGen/GenCC terminology, collaborative expert curation, and full
programmatic access through a public application programming interface (API) that
software can query directly.
Here, we present SysNDD (Figure 1), an extensive further development of the previous
SysID database18 with a new database concept, data model, and infrastructure. We
use this resource, structured around gene-inheritance-disease entities, to delineate the
current NDD landscape and to ask whether NDDs still resolve into the coherent
phenotypic and functional modules previously described for intellectual disability18.
Four questions guide the analysis: how many NDD genes are known and how the
catalog grows; how SysNDD compares with other gene resources; which phenotypes
and variant types are recorded; and whether clinically similar disorders involve genes
that interact molecularly.


Figure 1: The SysNDD concept, curation approach, and tools. a, Curation
workflow: evidence from literature is expert-curated (including annotation of
phenotypes, variant and inheritance data), assigned to one of four evidence categories
(Definitive, Moderate, Limited, or Refuted), and re-reviewed by ERN-ITHACA experts
on an ongoing basis; all records are standardized to community ontologies (HGNC,
HPO, OMIM, MONDO, and VariO). b, The curation unit is the entity, an immutable
gene-inheritance-disease triple rather than a gene-level record; one gene may yield
several entities, including dual-inheritance (Gene 1) or X-linked (Gene 2) associations.
c, NDD-associated entities by evidence category (bar length proportional to entity
count, linear axis): 2,043 Definitive, 226 Moderate, 1,479 Limited and 7 Refuted; the 3
uncategorized NDD entities are not shown. d, The openly licensed database (4,275
entities, 3,273 genes, 4,932 publications; CC BY 4.0 data) is accessible through a web
application, a documented REST API, and a read-only Model Context Protocol server.
Data: SysNDD API v0.38.1 (accessed September 21, 2026).


Methods
The entity data model
SysNDD is based on the “entity” concept (Figure 1b): a fixed triple of one gene, one
mode of inheritance and one disease, in which pathogenic variants in that gene cause
that disease through that inheritance pattern. Entities use standard identifiers: HUGO
Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) for genes19, Human Phenotype Ontology
(HPO) for inheritance20, OMIM for disease names10, and Mondo Disease Ontology
(MONDO) where no OMIM entry exists21. Each entity carries an evidence category
(Definitive, Moderate, Limited, or Refuted; Table S1) reflecting the strength of the
gene-disease association at the time of curation. Entities for non-NDD diseases linked
to an NDD-associated gene are tagged “Not applicable”, since they fall outside the
NDD evidence categories, and are kept for completeness. Entities are annotated with
38 HPO phenotype categories, published literature references, variant types and
consequences using the Variation Ontology (VariO)22, and a textual summary. Variant
annotations are assigned by curators from the primary literature. Alongside the curated
entities, the web interface displays external reference data for the same gene, namely
gnomAD gene constraint metrics23 and ClinVar variant records24; these data are not
imported into the curated entity. Curation history is retained for each entity. Re-review
adds new review and status records, and the newly approved status becomes the
active one. Entities are never deleted. Associations that no longer meet the criteria are
demoted or reclassified as Refuted and remain visible with their status history.
Duplicate or superseded entities are deactivated, withdrawn from public views, and
linked to their replacement.
Data curation and review process
SysNDD is maintained through continuous manual curation (Figure 1a). New
gene-disease associations are added as they appear in the literature. All entities,
beginning with those transferred from the previous SysID database, then undergo
systematic re-review by experts of the European Reference Network for Rare
Malformation Syndromes, Intellectual and Other Neurodevelopmental Disorders


(ERN-ITHACA; see Web Resources). During re-review, expert curators reassess
evidence categories against current evidence, update HPO phenotype annotations to
reflect new clinical data, verify inheritance modes, and add references from recent case
reports and large-scale studies. Detailed curation criteria and re-review rules are
available in the online SysNDD documentation (see Web Resources). A submitted
review becomes public only after approval. Curators in senior roles may approve their
own submissions; all other submissions require approval by a second curator.
The SysNDD toolkit
SysNDD is freely accessible online (Figure 1d; see Web Resources). The web
application offers tabular views of entities, genes, phenotypes, and diagnostic panels,
with search, filter, and download functions, and a Gene Networks view for exploring the
functional clusters and their enrichment tables (Supplemental Methods). Role-gated
pages support expert re-review, curator approval, and administration; their access and
data-control boundaries are summarized in Table S2. Software can query the same
records through the documented public API, and artificial intelligence (AI) assistants
can retrieve and cite them through a read-only Model Context Protocol interface.
SysNDD evidence categories also serve as training labels for NDDScore, an
exploratory genome-wide prediction layer developed separately from curation.
NDDScore predicts NDD association, inheritance, and phenotypes for protein-coding
genes without altering curated evidence (Table S3).
Phenotype clustering and functional analyses
To address the fourth question, we clustered the phenotype and functional axes
separately and then tested their overlap. Phenotype clustering was performed on
Definitive entities with HPO annotations, each encoded by the presence or absence of
the 38 HPO phenotype categories. Categories present in fewer than 5% or more than
95% of these entities barely distinguish one entity from another and were excluded
(prevalence filtering), leaving 30 HPO categories. The retained binary categories were
reduced by multiple correspondence analysis and clustered by hierarchical clustering
on principal components25,26. The number of clusters was set to the value of k at which


the step from k − 1 to k clusters gave the largest proportional drop in within-cluster
inertia.
Functional clustering was based on the STRING v11.5 functional-association
network27, whose separately scored evidence channels can be excluded individually.
To limit literature co-mention bias, we excluded the text-mining channel and applied
weighted Leiden community detection28 to an experimental-plus-database network.
Phenotype clusters are defined over gene-disease entities, whereas functional clusters
are defined over genes. Correspondence was therefore tested at gene level: each
gene was counted once per phenotype cluster, regardless of how many of its entities
fell in that cluster, and only genes present in both clusterings were included. For each
pair of a phenotype cluster and a functional cluster, we tested whether they share more
or fewer genes than expected by chance, using a two-sided Fisher exact test with
Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all pairs and a size-preserving permutation test
as a robustness check. Overlap is reported as the Jaccard index, the share of genes
common to both clusters among all genes in either29. Cluster stability, separation, and
dependence on curated STRING annotations were evaluated as described in
Supplemental Methods. Full parameter settings, confidence-interval procedures, and
sensitivity analyses, including a Definitive-only membership check (Table S4), are
provided in Supplemental Methods.
Database comparison and gene count estimation
We compared SysNDD with seven other NDD gene resources: PanelApp,
Gene2Phenotype, OMIM (restricted to entries annotated with the HPO term
Neurodevelopmental abnormality, HP:0012759, or a descendant; “OMIM NDD”),
Radboudumc ID, OrphaID, SFARI Gene, and Geisinger NDD GeneHub10–13,30,31.
Resource records were mapped to HGNC gene symbols and onto SysNDD’s four
evidence categories with a conversion table (the crosswalk), which makes resources
with different grading scales, and ungraded gene lists, comparable. Genes that the
crosswalk places in the top category, including all genes from ungraded lists, are
termed crosswalk-Definitive. The compared records reflect the shared access date of
September 21, 2026. The resulting gene-by-resource table and the crosswalk are


browsable at https://sysndd.dbmr.unibe.ch/CurationComparisons. Pairwise cosine
similarities between binary gene-membership vectors were converted to cosine
distances and clustered by average linkage. Completeness was measured as the
coverage gap: the share of consensus genes missing from a resource when that
resource is excluded from the consensus. As an exploratory analysis, we treated the
compared resources as repeated samples from a single gene pool and applied the
Chao2 richness estimator32 to project the total number of NDD-associated genes with
its analytic 95% confidence interval. Sensitivity analyses left out one database at a
time and, separately, restricted the input to crosswalk-Definitive genes. Because
resource scope and curation networks overlap, the resources are not independent
samples, and each projection is descriptive, not a formal lower bound; full methods and
sensitivity analyses are provided in Supplemental Methods.
Results
A growing catalog in which recessive genes outnumber dominant
genes
SysNDD currently catalogs 4,275 gene-inheritance-disease entities (one entity per
gene, mode of inheritance, and disease) across 3,273 genes. Of these, 3,758 entities
across 3,271 genes are associated with NDDs (accessed September 21, 2026); the
other 517 entities record non-NDD disorders, and 2 genes have only such entities.
Regarding evidence level for NDD, 2,043 entities are classified as Definitive (1,838
genes; 1,162 autosomal recessive, 698 autosomal dominant, 170 X-linked, and 13 with
other inheritance modes), 226 as Moderate (179 genes), and 1,479 as Limited (1,248
genes), with 7 Refuted and 3 uncategorized associations (Figure 1c; inheritance
breakdown by evidence category in Figure 2).


Figure 2: Cumulative gene-disease associations in SysID/SysNDD from 2010 to
present. a, Cumulative number of gene-disease entities over time, grouped by
evidence category (Definitive, Moderate, Limited, or Refuted). Lines represent the
running total of entities at each time point at which new entries were added. b,
Cumulative number of gene-disease entities over time, grouped by inheritance pattern.
A gene may be represented by multiple entities with different inheritance patterns. By
evidence category, 2,014 genes have a recessive NDD association (1,094 Definitive,
97 Moderate, 822 Limited), 1,262 have a dominant association (639 Definitive, 90
Moderate, 528 Limited), and 200 have an X-linked association (140 Definitive, 12
Moderate, 46 Limited); each gene is counted once per inheritance pattern at the
strongest category it reaches for that pattern, and the few genes outside these three
categories hold only Refuted or uncategorized assertions for that pattern. c,
Cumulative number of unique genes associated with both autosomal dominant (AD)


and autosomal recessive (AR) NDDs. “First AD, then AR” denotes genes first
associated with an AD NDD that later acquired a second, AR association, while “first
AR, then AD” denotes genes first associated with an AR NDD that later acquired a
second, AD association. Currently, 220 genes have both AD and AR associations, with
124 in the first-AD-then-AR group and 96 in the first-AR-then-AD group. Data: SysNDD
API v0.38.1 (timeline accessed September 21, 2026).
Temporal trend analysis (Figure 2; Figure S1) shows substantial growth for both
autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant entities. Genes with recessive NDD
associations outnumber those with dominant associations (2,014 versus 1,262), and
200 genes have X-linked NDD associations. A total of 220 autosomal genes are
associated with both dominant and recessive NDDs (Figure 2c), 45 with Definitive
evidence for both entities. Of these dual-inheritance genes, 124 were first associated
with a dominant NDD and later gained a recessive association, whereas 96 followed
the reverse order. In SLC2A1 (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome; MIM: 606777) and DNM1
(developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 31A and 31B; MIM: 616346, 620352),
dominant and recessive variants cause the same or allelic disorders. In contrast, in
ACOX1, for example, they cause distinct diseases: recessive peroxisomal acyl-CoA
oxidase deficiency (MIM: 264470) and dominant, gain-of-function-associated Mitchell
syndrome (MIM: 618960). X-linked NDDs fit poorly into a dominant/recessive
dichotomy anyway, because their manifestation in either or both sexes depends on the
gene, the variant mechanism, and X-inactivation33. Most X-chromosomal NDD entities
in SysNDD therefore lack this attribution: of 238 such entities, 160 are recorded as
“X-linked other inheritance”, compared to distinct classification as X-linked recessive
inheritance for 61 and X-linked dominant inheritance for 17 entities, respectively. The X
chromosome carries relatively few genes, and X-linked NDDs often segregate in
families, thus allowing disease gene identification by linkage analysis and Sanger
sequencing screens already before high-throughput sequencing34. Many X-linked NDD
genes were therefore known before exome sequencing, which explains why X-linked
entities have grown only modestly in recent years (Figure 2b).
Gene-disease associations in SysNDD, as well as phenotypic and genotypic
annotations, are based on 4,932 peer-reviewed publications from 1966 to 2026 (Figure


S2). Annual counts of publications used for curation rose steeply through the 2010s,
with the broad adoption of exome and genome sequencing in clinical genetics, and
peaked at 496 publications in 2021. Counts for the most recent years (215 publications
in 2025) are still incomplete, because a publication is counted only once it has been
used to curate an entity. Ranked by the number of publications (Figure S2b), the
leading sources are the American Journal of Human Genetics (680), GeneReviews
(395 chapters, linked as review literature rather than primary references), and the
American Journal of Medical Genetics Part A (342).
SysNDD overlaps with, but is not subsumed by, other NDD gene
resources
Of the 3,271 NDD-associated genes in SysNDD, 83.1% are also listed by at least one
of seven other major curation efforts, whereas 552 genes with positive SysNDD
evidence are listed by none of them (21 Definitive, 23 Moderate, and 508 Limited;
Figure 3a). Among broadly scoped databases filtered for neurodevelopmental
phenotypes, PanelApp ID has the greatest gene overlap with SysNDD (2,105 genes),
followed by OMIM NDD (1,975 genes) and Gene2Phenotype DD (1,907 genes). The
smaller, manually curated cross-disorder Geisinger NDD GeneHub shares 1,241 of its
1,576 genes with SysNDD. Gene sets focused on ID or autism overlap with SysNDD to
varying degrees: Radboudumc ID shares 1,943 of its 2,010 genes, OrphaID (the
Orphanet ID gene list) 1,300 of 1,561, and SFARI 792 of 1,274. The portal states that
this gene list was curated in partnership with ERN-ITHACA and SysID30, SysNDD’s
predecessor, so the SysNDD–OrphaID overlap partly reflects shared curation
provenance rather than independent agreement.


Figure 3: Comparison of SysNDD with other neurodevelopmental disorder gene
databases. (a) UpSet plot35 showing gene overlaps between the four largest NDD
databases: SysNDD (3,271 genes), PanelApp (2,833), Gene2Phenotype (2,554), and
OMIM NDD (2,426). Bars are ordered by intersection size. Among the four resources
shown, 809 genes are unique to SysNDD; across all eight analyzed resources, 552
positive-evidence SysNDD genes are absent from all seven comparators (21 Definitive,
23 Moderate, and 508 Limited). All four resources share 1,465 genes. (b) Cosine


similarity heatmap with hierarchical clustering showing relationships between the four
databases. Databases with more similar gene content cluster together. Among these
four databases, SysNDD is most similar to OMIM NDD, while the closest pair overall is
PanelApp and Gene2Phenotype. Data: SysNDD API v0.38.1 (accessed September 21,
2026).
The most similar gene lists are those of Gene2Phenotype DD and PanelApp ID (cosine
similarity 0.79, where 1 means identical lists; Figure 3b; all eight resources in Figure
S3b), consistent with shared curation networks. SFARI is the least similar (similarity ~
0.3–0.43), reflecting its focus on autism, a specific NDD subset, whereas the
cross-disorder Geisinger NDD GeneHub is more similar (~ 0.43–0.58), consistent with
its broad neurodevelopmental scope. Across all eight compared resources, SysNDD is
most similar to the Radboudumc ID gene list, compatible with, but not proof of, shared
curation traditions and collaborative networks.
The Chao2 richness estimator, which infers how many genes remain unlisted from how
many appear in only one or two resources, projected about 6,865 NDD genes in total
(95% CI 6,639–7,126), against 5,166 observed across these resources (Figures S4
and S5). Of the genes listed by at least four other resources, only 4.8% were absent
from SysNDD (its coverage gap), a smaller gap than for any other compared resource
(Figure S6). When only crosswalk-Definitive genes are counted (genes in the top
category after mapping every resource onto the SysNDD scale), the ranking reverses:
Radboudumc ID (2.2%) and OMIM NDD (5.6%) have smaller four-database coverage
gaps than SysNDD (6.8%). Most genes behind this gap (80 of 92) are listed by
SysNDD at a lower category, among them SPAST and NPC1, whose degenerative
disorders involve variable or acquired cognitive impairment; only 12 are not listed as
NDD genes. The Definitive-only gap therefore mainly reflects stricter grading rather
than missing genes.
Beyond coverage, we assessed how well SysNDD’s evidence categories agree with
those of external gene-disease validity resources for co-curated gene-disease pairs,
collapsed to SysNDD’s four-category scale (Table S1; Figure S7). Of the 565
gene-disease pairs curated by both SysNDD and ClinGen, the prespecified primary
comparator, the two resources assigned the same evidence category to 72% and the


same or an adjacent category to 84.6%. Weighted tier agreement was 85.5% (Gwet’s
AC2 0.806, 95% CI 0.774–0.839). Cohen’s κ was nevertheless low (0.191), because
most co-curated pairs were rated Definitive by both resources, and κ penalizes this
skew even when agreement is high (Table S5). Gene2Phenotype and Genomics
England PanelApp showed similar agreement (AC2 0.833 and 0.837).
We then categorized all 158 SysNDD–ClinGen discordances by evidence type using a
large language model that read the primary curation records of both resources
(Supplemental Methods; Data S1). Of these, 51.3% were genuine disagreements
about the evidence category, and in 77.8% of these SysNDD held the higher evidence
category. The rest arose from the comparison rather than from the evidence, chiefly
from differing curation dates and disease scope. Of the 44 discordances attributed to
curation-date lag, SysNDD retained a lower category after ClinGen had promoted the
association in 39; 2 showed the reverse pattern, and the remainder could not be
assigned a direction. These lags typically spanned several years (Table S5). Blinded
expert re-review of a stratified 60-discordance sample agreed moderately with the
model (Cohen’s κ = 0.433), so these proportions are model-assisted estimates.
Recorded phenotypes portray NDDs as multisystem disorders, and
variant annotations follow molecular logic
We examined how the 38 annotated HPO phenotype categories are distributed across
the 3,758 NDD entities in SysNDD (14,545 total annotations; Figure 4a, Figure S8a).
The most frequent categories are “abnormality of the nervous system” (n=1,277),
“abnormality of brain morphology” (n=1,173), and “seizures” (n=1,143). “Behavioral
abnormality” (n=697) and “abnormality of the eye” (n=674) are also prevalent, while
“genitourinary abnormalities” (n=263) and “Progressive” (n=303) illustrate the
multisystem and sometimes (neuro)degenerative nature of NDDs. Intellectual disability
is recorded not by the base HPO term (HP:0001249) but by five ID severity categories,
which reflect the degree of cognitive impairment rather than accompanying phenotypes;
“intellectual disability, moderate” is the most frequent (n=1,051; Figure 4a).


Figure 4: Phenotype and variant type distributions and correlations in SysNDD.
a, Horizontal bar chart showing the frequency of Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)
phenotype categories across SysNDD entities (top 20 of 38 categories shown;
complete distribution in Figure S8). Categories are sorted by entity count in
descending order. Abnormality of the nervous system (HP:0000707) is the most
frequently annotated phenotype (n=1,277), followed by abnormality of brain
morphology (HP:0002011, n=1,173) and seizures (HP:0001250, n=1,143). b,
Distribution of variant types across entities (top 10 of 40 categories shown), classified
using the Variation Ontology (VariO). Among the specific classes, nonsynonymous
variation (VariO:0017, n=1,728) and protein truncation (VariO:0015, n=1,558) are the
most frequent. c, Phenotype correlation heatmap showing pairwise Pearson r between
binary phenotype-category presence vectors (the phi coefficient) among 12 selected
HPO categories. The lower triangle is shown; the unit diagonal and duplicate upper
triangle are masked. Highlighted cells indicate the mitochondrial-musculature


correlation (r =0.41) and the eye-hearing sensory correlation (r =0.24). Purple indicates
negative and orange positive association; panels c and d share a symmetric diverging
color scale spanning the wider of the two panels’ correlation ranges. Full 38-phenotype
matrix in Figure S10. d, Variant-consequence correlation heatmap over a curated
subset of 10 mechanistically interpretable Variation Ontology (VariO) classes with at
least 10 annotated entities. A strong, mechanistically interpretable association
(highlighted) links protein truncation / out-of-frame indel (r =0.48), consistent with
out-of-frame (frameshifting) indels producing truncated proteins. Color encoding and
triangular display are as in c. Full 40-category variant matrix in Figure S11. HPO and
VariO annotations are hierarchical and non-exclusive; the correlations are descriptive,
not causal. Data: SysNDD API v0.38.1 (accessed September 21, 2026).
We call an entity syndromic when at least one organ system outside the nervous
system is recorded (16 systems, each counted once; Supplemental Methods). Of the
2,017 Definitive NDD entities with at least one recorded phenotype, 1,688 (83.7%) are
syndromic by this definition, and 1,310 (64.9%) have two or more organ systems
involved. Craniofacial features, abnormal head size, and eye involvement are most
frequently annotated. Because micro- and macrocephaly may reflect brain involvement
rather than a separate organ system, we repeated the count without head size; the
syndromic share then falls to 78.8% (Figure S9). Features not reported in the literature
count as absent, so some entities classed as non-syndromic may in fact be syndromic.
SysNDD captures variant consequences and types using 40 VariO categories22
(10,072 total annotations; Figure 4b, Figure S8b). Among specific consequences,
“nonsynonymous variation” is most prevalent (n=1,728), followed by “protein truncation”
(n=1,558), “out-of-frame indel” (n=1,229), explicit “protein loss of function” (n=1,151),
and “affected splice site” (n=1,141). “Chromosomal deletion” (n=312), a VariO class
distinct from the indel classes, and gain-of-function effects (n=133) are also
documented. Because VariO annotations are hierarchical and non-exclusive, these
counts describe annotation patterns rather than frequencies of molecular mechanisms.
The annotations are curated from the primary literature and maintained separately from
the ClinVar24 records that SysNDD displays for the same gene, so the two sources may
differ.


Phenotype co-occurrence, measured as phi coefficients between the presence of two
categories across Definitive entities and reported descriptively (Supplemental
Methods), reveals biologically coherent correlations. Figure 4c shows 12 categories
selected manually to span neurological, sensory, organ-system, and clinical-course
features; the full 38-phenotype matrix is shown in Figure S10. “Abnormality of the
mitochondrion” correlates with “musculature abnormality” (r = 0.41) and with “age of
death” (r = 0.27), consistent with the severe clinical course of some mitochondrial
disorders. Weaker but expected pairings link “abnormality of the eye” with “hearing
impairment” (r = 0.24) and “seizures” with “abnormality of brain morphology” (r = 0.23).
Variant-consequence annotations show comparable internal coherence (Figure 4d; full
40-category matrix in Figure S11). Within the curated subset shown in Figure 4d, the
strongest positive associations follow the expected molecular logic, from a
frameshifting or splice-disrupting change to a truncated, non-functional protein:
affected splice site / out-of-frame indel (r = 0.52), protein truncation / out-of-frame indel
(r = 0.48), and protein loss of function / protein truncation (r = 0.37). The strongest
negative association, though modest, is protein gain of function / protein truncation (r =
-0.19), consistent with gain and loss of function being recorded as alternative rather
than co-occurring mechanisms. Together, the phenotype annotations portray NDDs as
multisystem disorders, and both phenotype and variant annotations show internally
coherent patterns, although variant mechanism is captured only coarsely for much of
the catalog.
Genes form distinct molecular clusters, whereas disorders form
broad phenotype groups
The two clustering approaches address different questions: phenotype clustering
groups gene-disease entities whose clinical presentations resemble one another,
whereas functional clustering groups genes whose protein products act together in the
cell, irrespective of the associated disorders. Comparing the two partitions tests a
long-standing proposal that phenotypically similar disorders often arise from variants in
functionally related genes36. Genes fell into 18 functional clusters (Figure 5a) and
Definitive entities into 3 broad phenotype clusters (PC1–3; Figure 5b; Tables S6 and


S7). Functional clusters keep their raw Leiden community numbers, so their labels are
not consecutive (e.g., FC69, FC301).
Figure 5: Functional clusters show selective, generally weak correspondence
with phenotype clusters. (a) STRING v11.5 functional-association network27 of
NDD-associated genes, partitioned by weighted Leiden community detection into 18
functional clusters. Each deterministic force-directed subnetwork37 shows its functional
theme, full membership count, and labeled representative gene; nodes are scaled by
displayed interaction degree. For legibility, the 2,601 clustered genes are represented
by the 10,000 strongest interactions, as a display subset of the graph used for
clustering. (b) Phenotype clusters from multiple correspondence analysis followed by
hierarchical clustering on the prevalence-filtered, category-level HPO representation of
Definitive entities: PC1, progressive/metabolic (n=341); PC2, intellectual
disability/seizures (n=1,122); and PC3, multisystem malformation (n=554). Node area
encodes cluster size, link width encodes the absolute correlation between the two
clusters’ memberships, and the layout is not a spatial embedding. (c) The PC–FC
correlation block is reconstructed directly from the memberships displayed in panels a


and b, using one binary membership bit per gene across the 1,517 genes of the
shared gene set. Rows show PC1–PC3 and columns show FC1–FC301 (raw Leiden
community numbers, hence non-consecutive); color encodes signed Pearson r. Black
outlines with coefficient labels mark the four associations discussed in the Results
(PC1–FC2, PC1–FC10, PC3–FC6, and PC2–FC17). They are among the 17 of 54
cells significant at q < 0.05; the other significant cells are not outlined. Associations
across the block are generally small (median |r |=0.05, maximum 0.30). Data: SysNDD
analysis release (API v0.38.1; accessed September 21, 2026).
The two axes behave very differently. Genes cluster much more strongly than expected
by chance: the modularity of the functional network (0.679) far exceeds that of
randomized networks in which every gene keeps its number of interactions (mean 0.22;
empirical p ≤ 0.005). The phenotype partition is reproducible under resampling
(bootstrap-Jaccard 0.935–0.947, where 1 means the same clusters on every resample).
It is, however, only weakly separated (mean silhouette 0.183, on a scale where 0
means no separation and 1 perfect separation), so there is no evidence of discrete
phenotype modules in this representation. Molecular interaction is thus the sharper
organizing axis, although the network partly re-encodes curated pathway annotation
that the phenotype side also draws on. Stability of the functional partition varies by
cluster: per-cluster bootstrap-Jaccard ranges from 0.326 in FC23 to 0.813 in FC10
(Table S7). Re-clustering on experimental evidence alone, without STRING’s
curated-database channel, still gave strong modularity (0.74, z = 206 against the same
null), but the resulting clusters agreed only moderately with the combined ones
(adjusted Rand index 0.39, where 1 means identical clusters; Figure S12).
The phenotype clusters capture broad clinical axes rather than fine syndromic groups.
PC1 (341 entities) gathers progressive, metabolic, and mitochondrial presentations and
is enriched for autosomal recessive inheritance; PC2 (1,122 entities) is dominated by
intellectual disability, behavioral abnormalities, and seizures; and PC3 (554 entities) is
enriched for genitourinary, skeletal, cardiac, facial, and renal abnormalities and short
stature. PC2 and PC3 are both enriched for autosomal dominant inheritance. All of
them are weakly separated (per-cluster silhouettes 0.05–0.251) in this HPO
representation. The partition also depends on how missing annotations are treated: it


is not reproduced when unrecorded phenotypes are treated as unknown rather than
absent (adjusted Rand index near zero). The partition was largely retained when the
intellectual disability severity grades were removed or prevalence filtering was omitted
(adjusted Rand index 0.75 and 0.83; Supplemental Methods). The 18 text-mining-free
functional clusters, by contrast, resolve recognizable molecular themes.
Representative genes include NDUFS1 and ACAD9 (mitochondrial function); ARID1B,
CHD7, and KMT2D (chromatin regulation); GRIN1 and SYNGAP1 (synaptic signaling);
CEP290 (ciliary transition zone); and PIGA and PIGN (glycosylation). All themes are
listed in Table S7. A further 550 NDD genes have no interaction above the score
threshold once the text-mining channel is excluded and therefore belong to no cluster.
The molecular composition of the phenotype clusters, which their construction does not
use, is tested next.
Clinical groups correspond to molecular clusters only selectively
We tested whether phenotype clusters align with functional clusters across 54 pairwise
comparisons (Figure 5c; Tables S6 and S7) among the 1,517 genes present in both
clusterings (1,823 genes carry a phenotype cluster and 2,601 a functional cluster). Of
the 54 cells, 17 were significant (q < 0.05; 9 enrichments and 8 depletions), but the
overlaps were modest. The most readily interpretable coupling was the
near-definitional PC1–FC2 link between the progressive/metabolic phenotype cluster
and the mitochondrial cluster (OR=11.05, 95% CI 6.83 to 17.87, Jaccard=0.182,
q=<0.001; full test statistics in Data S1). An odds ratio of this size means that
progressive/metabolic-cluster genes are many times over-represented in the
mitochondrial cluster, whereas the low Jaccard index means that the two groupings
share only a minority of their genes.
Beyond this definitional axis, the progressive/metabolic cluster was also enriched for
the small-molecule-metabolism cluster (PC1–FC10; OR=3.37, Jaccard=0.165). The
multisystem-malformation cluster was enriched for the nuclear/chromatin cluster
(PC3–FC6; OR=2.77, Jaccard=0.216), consistent with chromatin regulators such as
ARID1B, CHD7, and KMT2D in that cluster. Likewise, the intellectual disability/seizure
cluster was enriched for the neuronal-signaling and membrane-trafficking clusters


(PC2–FC4, OR=1.82; PC2–FC17, OR=4.91). Phenotype clusters therefore do not map
one-to-one onto molecular modules. Of the couplings highlighted in Figure 5c, 3 persist
after removing STRING’s curated-database channel (Supplemental Methods), whereas
the small-molecule-metabolism link remains specific to the combined network.
Because this comparison inherits the weak phenotype partition, we also tested each
functional cluster against the 30 active phenotype categories (Figure S13). Of the 540
cells, 110 deviated from expectation (q < 0.05), including kidney abnormalities in the
ciliary cluster and microcephaly in the DNA-repair cluster. Overall, the two axes
correspond only partially: significant enrichments or depletions occur in a minority of
cluster pairs, individual overlaps are modest, and the most prominent coupling,
PC1–FC2, is near-definitional.
Discussion
SysNDD represents each neurodevelopmental gene-disease association as a
versioned gene-inheritance-disease entity with a recorded evidence category and
supporting publications. This structure lets clinicians and researchers query individual
associations, assemble or audit diagnostic panels, analyze the catalog systematically,
and trace when and why an assessment changed.
Curation in SysNDD began with the transition from SysID on May 7, 2022. Since then,
the database has added 820 gene-disease associations (762 unique genes), averaging
187 associations and 174 genes per year. Over the same period, 689 re-reviews
(systematic expert reassessments, beginning with entries transferred from SysID) were
completed, and the annotations of 1,496 entities and the status of 837 entities were
updated, including for dual-inheritance patterns and phenotypic expansions. These
activities show that continuous curation involves both expanding the catalog and
reassessing existing associations.
The clinically most relevant differences between resources involve Definitive and
Moderate evidence level categorization. SysNDD includes 21 Definitive and 23
Moderate genes absent from every other comparison resource. These
higher-confidence associations illustrate the complementary coverage of


expert-curated resources8. However, their absence from another resource does not
necessarily indicate disagreement, as resources differ in scope, inclusion criteria,
evidence frameworks, and update schedules. The 508 SysNDD-only Limited genes
include early and historical candidate associations that require continuing re-review;
where current criteria are no longer met, they are demoted or reclassified as Refuted
rather than removed. A continuously maintained resource can promote, demote, or
refute associations as evidence changes17, whereas a published list begins aging at
publication. Continuous maintenance does not remove reassessment lag, however: in
most date-lag discordances with ClinGen, SysNDD was behind, which argues for
periodic cross-resource review.
The distribution of inheritance modes has implications for diagnostic strategies and
genetic counseling. Although autosomal dominant NDDs associated with de novo
variants predominate in non-consanguineous diagnostic cohorts1, autosomal recessive
entities outnumber autosomal dominant entities in SysNDD, consistent with the even
more pronounced genetic heterogeneity of recessive NDDs38. After proband-only
sequencing, recessive diagnoses may require parental testing or long-read data to
phase variants and establish compound heterozygosity. The substantial fraction of de
novo dominant diagnoses, in turn, helps explain the higher diagnostic yield of
trio-based than proband-only sequencing1,39. In the 220 genes with both dominant and
recessive entities, a heterozygous variant may be causal or indicate only carrier status,
so interpretation and counseling must be mode-specific. X-linked labels are similarly
imprecise. Females with heterozygous pathogenic variants in genes associated with
only X-linked recessive NDDs may be symptomatic, and female predominance in some
X-linked dominant disorders may reflect male lethality33,40.
Inheritance mode and variant mechanism must also be interpreted together.
Loss-of-function variants contribute to both recessive and dominant NDDs, through
biallelic loss of function in recessive disorders and haploinsufficiency in many dominant
disorders. Common examples of disease genes with haploinsufficiency mechanisms
include ARID1B (Coffin-Siris syndrome 1; MIM: 135900), ANKRD11 (KBG syndrome;
MIM: 148050), and SYNGAP1 (intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal
dominant 5; MIM: 612621), whereas other dominant NDD genes act through


gain-of-function, dominant-negative, or other mechanisms41,42, and in some genes,
such as ACOX1, different mechanisms cause distinct disorders. Copy-number changes
and other structural variants add another layer and may be detected by exome-based
dosage analysis43, genome sequencing, or targeted assays. SysNDD records VariO
classes for each entity, allowing molecular mechanism to be considered alongside
inheritance and clinical interpretation.
In the current catalog, molecular modules are well separated, whereas disorder-level
HPO profiles form broad, overlapping groups. Part of this asymmetry reflects
resolution: each disorder is described by 30 binary phenotype categories, whereas
each gene is placed by weighted interactions with its partners. Aggregation of
phenotypes across individuals within a disorder and incomplete phenotype annotation
may further limit correspondence between phenotypic and molecular groupings, as
anticipated by Kochinke et al. for sparse disorder-level phenotyping18. These clusters
and their correspondence are descriptive. They neither define a phenotype taxonomy
nor establish causal relationships between molecular modules and phenotypes. For
now, molecular modules offer the more robust grouping of NDD genes, and phenotype
groups are best read as broad clinical context until patient-level phenotypes allow a
finer comparison.
SysNDD’s distinct contribution lies in its independent primary curation of versioned
gene-inheritance-disease entities, including separate entities for distinct disease
associations or modes of inheritance of the same gene. This complements GenCC’s
harmonization of assertions from member groups16. The structured annotations
associated with these entities support NDD-scale phenotype-function analyses: shared
pathways can underlie overlapping, pleiotropic phenotypes44,45, and NDD-associated
genes converge in co-expression and interaction modules46,47.
SysNDD evidence categories also provide the training labels for NDDScore, the
exploratory genome-wide prediction layer: genes with Definitive or Moderate
associations form its positive reference set. On held-out test data, its association model
achieved an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve of 0.89 (0.5 is
chance and 1 perfect ranking). Applied to the 16,088 genes not curated in SysNDD, it
ranked MAU2, the obligate partner of NIPBL in cohesin loading, highest. MAU2 was


not part of the training data and was only later included in SysNDD, after a recent
report established it as a new Cornelia de Lange syndrome gene48, consistent with the
predicted autosomal dominant inheritance and phenotypes. This is a post hoc
observation, not an independent validation.
Disorder-level HPO annotations do not retain patient-level detail and depend on what
the literature reports and curators capture, so they cannot show how features are
distributed across individuals. Phenotypes recorded per patient in a standardized,
machine-readable form could test whether the same groupings emerge in individuals49.
The functional analyses have a related limit: they include only genes with interaction
evidence beyond co-mention in the literature, and because the network partly draws on
known pathway annotations, its modules and their phenotype associations are not fully
independent of existing knowledge.
Because entities are versioned and record phenotype, inheritance, and variant
consequence in one structure, SysNDD supports analyses beyond a pure gene list.
Genes retrieved by a combination of phenotype categories can be intersected with
functional modules to nominate mechanisms for experimental follow-up, as proposed
for intellectual disability modules18; the recovery of the known kidney involvement of
ciliopathy genes (Figure S13) shows that such intersections return expected biology.
These queries generate hypotheses and inherit the limits of literature-derived,
disorder-level annotation. Finally, both Chao2 projections indicate that a substantial
share of NDD genes remains unlisted; continued curation will test them prospectively,
as it will the NDDScore rankings.
Data and code availability
The SysNDD database is freely accessible at https://sysndd.dbmr.unibe.ch (permanent
redirect: https://sysndd.org). All data are available through the public API at
https://sysndd.dbmr.unibe.ch/API with full OpenAPI/Swagger documentation. The
SysNDD web application source is publicly available at
https://github.com/berntpopp/sysndd, and the key analysis software and packages are
listed in Table S8. Database content is released under the Creative Commons


Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license
(https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
This paper analyzes existing, publicly available data: the SysNDD records and analysis
releases served by API v0.38.1 on the access dates given in the figure legends and
Supplemental Methods. Source URLs and access dates are listed in Table S9. The
underlying analysis tables are provided as Data S1, a workbook with one worksheet
per table and a README sheet describing each. The separately developed NDDScore
prediction release is freely available at https://sysndd.dbmr.unibe.ch/NDDScore and
archived at Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20258026).
